title: Creating and Using a Class
objective: Define a class, initialize it with __init__(), and call a method on an instance you create from it.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose, examples, and exercises are original Code Forge material using an original theme, not the book's example classes.

paragraphs: A class is a blueprint for creating objects that bundle data and behavior together. Once you define a class, you can create as many independent instances from it as you need, and each instance keeps its own copy of the data described by the blueprint.

Every class that stores data on its instances defines a special method named __init__(). Python calls __init__() automatically whenever you create a new instance, so it is the natural place to set up whatever information that instance needs to start out with.

Inside a class, the first parameter of every method is conventionally named self. self is how an instance refers to itself, and Python supplies it automatically — you never pass it in yourself when calling a method on an instance.
explanation.rule: Define a class with class ClassName:, set up instance data in __init__(), then create an instance and call its methods with dot notation.

examples.title: Defining and Using a Class
examples.note: Apprentice("Mira", "swordsmithing") triggers __init__() automatically, storing both arguments on self. Calling first_apprentice.introduce() then runs that method for this one instance.

checks.question: What does self refer to inside a class's method?
options: The specific instance the method is being called on.
The class itself, not any particular instance.
A built-in Python keyword that means nothing.
The last object created from any class.

feedback.correct: Correct — self always refers to the instance the method was called on.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. self stands in for whichever instance called the method.

assignment.title: Forge Badge
assignment.brief: Write a Badge class that stores a rank and can display it.
requirements: Implement __init__(self, rank) that stores rank as self.rank.
Implement a method display() that prints f"Badge rank: {self.rank}".
Create an instance of Badge and call display() on it.
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    _cf_badge = Badge("Journeyman")
    _cf_badge.display()
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))

hints: Start with class Badge: to define the class itself.
__init__(self, rank) runs automatically when you create a new Badge — use it to store rank on self.rank.
display() only needs self as a parameter; use an f-string to print self.rank.
After the class is defined, create an instance with Badge("Novice") and then call .display() on that instance.
